text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday's Albanian newspapers. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The editorial says that the arrival of a U.S. military adviser to Albanian Defence Minister Safet Zhulali is a matter of routine protocol and not an indication of any improvement in tense U.S.-Albania relations.

- The Gjallica company has split into two, with its president inheriting its $300 million loan operation. The company has promised to start re-paying investors the eight percent monthly return it offered them initially from Jan 15.

- The opposition Democratic Alliance Party continues to accuse the ruling Democratic Party of financing its general election campaign with money from alleged pyramid schemes, including one run by the Gjallica company.
- Sources within the ruling Democratic Party confirmed they have decided to eject Azem Hajdari, a founding member turned trade union leader who has supported anti-government strikes.

- The Albanian branch of the human rights group Helsinki Committee has protested to local authorities in Berat, southern Albania, about the expulsion of Romany gypsies from their homes to provide more space for Albanians to build houses.
- The "Chinese influenza" virus, an unusual epidemic occurring every 14 years, has struck Albania.
- Sude, the notorious head of an alleged pyramid scheme which has stopped paying returns to depositors says she does not know when she will be able to pay them back.
- An alleged small pyramid scheme has collapsed in the southern town of Kucove, owing one million dollars to depositors.
- The European Union's PHARE programme, which offers technical aid to East European countries, has allocated seven million ECUs to Albania's health system.
- Inflation in 1996 rose to 17.4 percent, compared with 6.01 percent in the same period in 1995. It is now 50 percent more expensive to buy bread.
